implementation_notes: C++17 puts the algebra in the standard library: one plain struct per operation and `using Expr = std::variant<Const, Add, Get, Log>` (children behind `std::unique_ptr<Expr>` to break the recursion), with `std::visit(overloaded{...}, expr.node)` as the interpreter - the abstract Expression hierarchy and its virtual `interpret` are replaced by a closed variant plus one overload per alternative. The overload set is total by construction: adding an alternative makes every `std::visit` fail to instantiate until each interpreter handles it, which is C++'s closest analogue of exhaustive matching. Keep the classic hierarchy when nodes carry behaviour or invariants, or when third parties must extend the algebra, since variant alternatives cannot be added externally.
pitfalls: std::variant identifies alternatives by type: two operations with identical members collapse into one alternative unless one is wrapped or tagged.
Recursive variants need indirection (unique_ptr or a box type); a variant that contains itself directly does not compile.
A missing overload makes std::visit a wall of template errors, so keep overload sets small and the helpers named.
unique_ptr children make programs move-only: a copy for logging requires an explicit clone/walk.

variants.name: Boost.Proto expression templates (compile-time programs)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++17 route - still the right one for compile-time DSLs - builds the program as an expression template: overloaded operators compose typed nodes and a Proto grammar/transform interprets the tree at compile time, so evaluation can be inlined and no runtime data structure is allocated. Where the std::variant form pays per-node allocation and std::visit dispatch, expression templates pay in compile time and template diagnostics, and the language is limited to what C++ operator syntax can express. Choose them for math, query or unit DSLs evaluated at compile time, not for programs that must be logged, stored, serialized or dispatched at runtime.
pitfalls: Expression templates are compile-time data: a program cannot be read back, serialized or changed at run time - the opposite trade from std::variant.
Diagnostics for a malformed expression are pages of template errors; constrain the grammar early to keep messages usable.
